# Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman was born in 1953 to a Jewish family in New York City and showed an early interest in computers, reading manuals for the IBM 7094 as a pre-teen. He studied at Harvard University and later attended MIT, where he worked as a programmer at the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory from 1971. His early work included developing TECO and Emacs, and he became an ardent critic of restricted computer access when MIT installed a password control system in 1977.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, as software manufacturers began restricting copying and source code distribution, Stallman declared this a "crime against humanity." In 1984, he quit MIT to work full-time on the GNU project, aiming to create a free operating system compatible with Unix. He founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 and popularized the concept of "copyleft," first implemented in the Emacs General Public License and later in the GNU General Public License (GPL). Stallman argues that "free software" is a moral imperative for user freedom, distinguishing it from "open source," which he views merely as a development model. He advocates for the term "GNU/Linux" to acknowledge the GNU project's role in the operating system.
Stallman has been an outspoken activist for free software since the early 1990s, influencing governments and organizations to adopt free software. He has participated in protests against proprietary software, digital rights management, and software patents, and has advocated for reduced copyright terms. His personal life includes being childfree, atheistic, and living in Boston. He has received numerous honors, including a MacArthur Fellowship in 1990 and a National Academy of Engineering membership in 2002. In September 2023, he was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma but is in remission.
